lead: Every mechanics problem starts the same way: mark a boundary, add the forces crossing it, and write ΣF = dp/dt. Newton's three laws make this one recipe work for a stone and for a rocket. Forces inside a system come in equal and opposite pairs and cancel, so with no outside force the total momentum stays fixed. The same bookkeeping gives conservation of energy and of angular momentum. Orbits, braking, launches and a cricket stroke all follow from it.
prereq: You need school-level Newton's laws, vector components, and the derivative as a rate of change. Stress and strain start fresh in 1.2.

sections.h3: Force, inertia and the three laws

blocks.text: A force is a push or pull that changes a body's velocity, measured in newtons (N); 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A body's resistance to change of velocity is inertia, measured by its mass m in kilograms.
First law: with zero net force a body stays at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line. It cannot be proved from anything simpler; it defines the frames where the other two laws hold.
Second law: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass this is ΣF = m a.
ΣF = dp/dt = m a   (m constant)
blocks.where: ΣF is the net external force in N; p = m v is momentum in kg·m/s; v is velocity in m/s; t is time in s; a = dv/dt is acceleration in m/s².

blocks.text: A force acting for a short time gives an impulse: ΣF Δt = Δp. That is how a bat changes a ball's momentum in milliseconds.
Third law: if A pushes B, B pushes A with equal magnitude along the same line, opposite direction, same type of force. The two act on different bodies.

items: Momentum and force are vectors: p = m v points along v; resolve forces into components and add.
A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m/s carries p = 4.8 kg·m/s.

sections.h3: Frames of reference and Galilean transformation

blocks.text: An inertial frame is one where the first law holds: a free body moves in a straight line at constant speed. Ground-fixed frames are nearly inertial; a braking bus is not.
In a non-inertial frame we add a pseudo force −m A, with A the frame's acceleration. In a bus braking at 2 m/s² a 60 kg passenger feels 60 × 2 = 120 N forward.
Galilean transformation: frame S′ moves at constant velocity v along x relative to S; time is the same in both.
x′ = x − v t,   u′ = u − v,   t′ = t
blocks.where: x, u are position and velocity in S; x′, u′ the same in S′; v is the constant velocity of S′ along x, in m/s.

blocks.text: Velocities add like arrows. A swimmer of speed c in still water crossing a river of width d flowing at v, aiming straight across, takes d/c and drifts v d/c downstream. To land opposite, aim upstream; the crossing then takes d/√(c² − v²).
No experiment inside a smoothly moving closed train reveals its speed. This fails near light speed — see 1.7.

sections.h3: Conservation of momentum and the centre of mass

blocks.text: Split every force on a system into internal (between its parts) and external (from outside). By the third law internal forces come in equal, opposite pairs on the same line and cancel.
ΣF_ext = dP/dt,   P = Σ mᵢ vᵢ
blocks.where: ΣF_ext is the vector sum of external forces in N; P is total momentum in kg·m/s; mᵢ, vᵢ are the mass and velocity of the i-th part.

blocks.text: If ΣF_ext = 0 then P is constant: conservation of linear momentum. It holds for collisions, explosions and recoil even when the internal forces are violent and unknown.
Recoil: a gun of mass M firing a bullet of mass m at speed v moves back at V = m v / M, since the total momentum started at zero.
F = u R
blocks.where: F is rocket thrust in N; u is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket in m/s; R = −dm/dt is the mass loss rate in kg/s.

blocks.text: Centre of mass: R_cm = (Σ mᵢ rᵢ)/Σ mᵢ. For a uniform rod of length L with x = 0 at one end, x_cm = (1/M)∫₀^L (M/L) x dx = L/2. It moves as if all the mass and all external forces sat there.
Work along a path is W = ∫F·dr; for a constant force along the motion W = F d cos θ. The unit is the joule (J) = 1 N·m.
W_net = ½ m v² − ½ m u²
blocks.where: W_net is total work by all forces in J; m is mass in kg; u, v are initial and final speeds in m/s. This is the work–energy theorem.

blocks.text: A conservative force stores potential energy U with F = −dU/dx, and then KE + U is constant. Friction is not conservative: its work depends on the path and it turns mechanical energy into heat.
L = r × p,   τ = dL/dt
blocks.where: L is angular momentum in kg·m²/s, magnitude m v r sin θ; r is the position vector from the origin in m; τ is torque in N·m. If Στ = 0, L stays constant.

blocks.text: A planet feels only the Sun's pull along the joining line, so torque about the Sun is zero and L is fixed. Area swept per second is L/(2m), constant — Kepler's second law.
F = G M m / r²,   T² = 4π² a³ / (G M)
blocks.where: F is gravitational attraction in N; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²; M, m are masses in kg; r is separation in m; T is orbital period in s; a is semi-major axis in m.

items: Lever: F₁ d₁ = F₂ d₂ about the fulcrum.
Archimedes: upthrust = weight of fluid displaced.
Copernican model: the Sun sits at the centre.
Kepler: elliptical orbits; equal areas in equal times; T² ∝ a³.

figure.caption: Read top to bottom: mark the system, list outside forces, apply the second law, set the net outside force to zero to read off constant momentum.

spec.title: One rule for any system
spec.aria: A five-step flow: mark the system, list external forces, apply ΣF = dp/dt, set the net external force to zero, and read off constant momentum because internal pairs cancel.

examples.question: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg arrives at the bat at 30 m/s and leaves along the same line in the opposite direction at 20 m/s. Contact lasts 0.010 s. Take the incoming direction as positive. (a) Find the momentum before and after the stroke. (b) Find the change in momentum. (c) Find the average force on the ball.
steps: Data with signs: m = 0.16 kg, u = +30 m/s, v = −20 m/s, Δt = 0.010 s.
Before: p₁ = 0.16 × 30 = 4.8 kg·m/s, towards the bat.
After: p₂ = 0.16 × (−20) = −3.2 kg·m/s, back towards the bowler.
Change: Δp = −3.2 − 4.8 = −8.0 kg·m/s; the magnitude 8.0 is 4.8 + 3.2, because the ball reversed.
The minus sign says the force points opposite to the incoming ball.
examples.answer: The momentum changes by −8.0 kg·m/s and the bat exerts an average force of −800 N, i.e. 800 N directed opposite to the incoming ball.
examples.check:
m = 0.16
u = 30.0
v = -20.0
dt = 0.010
p1 = round(m * u, 2)
p2 = round(m * v, 2)
dp = round(p2 - p1, 2)
F = round(dp / dt, 2)
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(dp)
print(F)

traps: Momentum is a vector. On reversal the change is 4.8 + 3.2 = 8.0 kg·m/s, not 4.8 − 3.2.
Internal forces cancel only for the whole system; for one part they are the only forces acting.
ΣF = dp/dt uses the net external force. A train at steady 80 km/h has many forces but their sum is zero.
Rocket thrust uses the exhaust speed relative to the rocket, never speed from the ground.
Kepler's second law means constant angular momentum: speed is largest nearest the Sun, not constant around the orbit.

quiz.q: State Newton's third law. Why can internal forces not change the total momentum of a system?
quiz.a: Action and reaction are equal, opposite, along the same line, on different bodies. Inside a system they pair to zero, so only external forces appear in ΣF_ext = dP/dt.

quiz.q: A book rests on a table. Its weight and the table's upward push are equal and opposite. Are they an action–reaction pair? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Both act on the book and cancel because its acceleration is zero. The reaction to the book's weight is the book pulling the Earth up; the reaction to the table's push is the book pressing down on the table.

quiz.q: A 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s brakes uniformly to rest in 3.0 s. Find the average braking force.
A rocket burns fuel at 20 kg/s and ejects the gas at 2.5 km/s relative to the rocket. Find the thrust.
A pendulum hangs from the roof of a bus accelerating at A = 2 m/s². Find the angle it makes with the vertical, and say whether the bus frame is inertial.
quiz.a: In the bus frame a pseudo force −m A acts, so tan θ = A/g = 2/9.8 = 0.204, θ ≈ 11.5°. The bus frame is non-inertial; from the ground T sin θ = m A and T cos θ = m g give the same angle.

quiz.q: A swimmer aims straight across a river and never lands directly opposite the starting point. Why, and what must the swimmer do to land opposite?
quiz.a: The current carries the swimmer downstream while crossing at speed c: time d/c, drift v d/c. Landing opposite needs an upstream component equal to v, so aim upstream; the crossing then takes d/√(c² − v²).

quiz.q: A satellite in an elliptical orbit is at r₁ = 7.0 × 10⁶ m from the Earth's centre with speed 9.0 × 10³ m/s. Find its speed at the farthest point, r₂ = 1.4 × 10⁷ m.
quiz.a: The force is central, so L is conserved; at the apsides v ⊥ r, so r₁ v₁ = r₂ v₂. Hence v₂ = (7.0 × 10⁶ × 9.0 × 10³)/(1.4 × 10⁷) = 4.5 × 10³ m/s.

beyond: Not for the exam. Launch vehicles are sized by this momentum bookkeeping: F = u R fixes the burn rate for a given exhaust speed, and staging drops dead mass. Spacecraft also use gravity assists (central-force scattering) and ion thrusters giving tiny thrust for months. Search for the rocket equation, specific impulse and Hohmann transfer orbit. The same centre-of-mass and momentum equations keep walking robots and simulated bodies stable.
